e-9866.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of X
e-9866.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x = t-\sin t, \quad y = 1-\cos t, \quad t\in \left[0,\pi\right].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis?
e-9866.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=0$ to $t_2=\pi.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\sin^2 t +\cos^2 t= 1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{3}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

e-9867.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y
e-9867.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x = \sin t, \quad y = e^t, \quad t\in \left[0,1\right].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis?
e-9867.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} x \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=0$ to $t_2=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

e-9869.knowledge_point: Computing a Surface Area of Revolution
e-9869.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x = 1+3t, \quad y = 2t^{3/2}, \quad t\in \left[0,1\right].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis.
e-9869.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} x \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=0$ to $t_2=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)=3 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3/2})=3{t}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{{(3)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{1/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{9+9t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{9(1+t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\cdot 3\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u = 1+t.$ Then, $1+3t=3u-2$ and $\textrm{d}u = \textrm d t.$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.

| **$t$** | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}(3u-2)\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}(3{u}^{3/2}-2{u}^{1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\pi \cdot {[\frac{6{u}^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{4{u}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =6\pi [(\frac{6({2}^{5/2})}{5}-\frac{4({2}^{3/2})}{3})-(\frac{6}{5}-\frac{4}{3})] \\  & =6\pi [(\frac{24\sqrt{2}}{5}-\frac{8\sqrt{2}}{3})-(\frac{6}{5}-\frac{4}{3})] \\  & =6\pi [\frac{32\sqrt{2}}{15}+\frac{2}{15}] \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{5}(16\sqrt{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 1
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=cos⁡2t,y=cos⁡t,t∈[0,π4]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
π∫0π/4cos2⁡tsin⁡t16cos2⁡t−1dt
b
π∫0π/4cos2⁡tsin⁡t9sin2⁡t−1dt
c
2π∫0π/4cos2⁡tsin⁡t8cos2⁡t+1dt
d
2π∫0π/4cos⁡tsin⁡t16cos2⁡t+1dt
e
2π∫0π/4cos⁡tsin2⁡t9cos2⁡t+1dt
Submit

decision.explanation: For rotation about the x-axis, S=2π∫y√((x′)²+(y′)²) dt. Here x′=-2sin(2t)=-4sin(t)cos(t) and y′=-sin(t), so the speed is sin(t)√(16cos²(t)+1), since sin(t)≥0 on [0,π/4]. Multiplying by y=cos(t) gives option d.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{4}].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡2t=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t(16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot |\operatorname{sin}⁡t|\cdot \sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=cos⁡2t,y=cos⁡t,t∈[0,π4]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
π∫0π/4cos2⁡tsin⁡t16cos2⁡t−1dt
b
π∫0π/4cos2⁡tsin⁡t9sin2⁡t−1dt
c
2π∫0π/4cos2⁡tsin⁡t8cos2⁡t+1dt
d
2π∫0π/4cos⁡tsin⁡t16cos2⁡t+1dt
e
2π∫0π/4cos⁡tsin2⁡t9cos2⁡t+1dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=π4.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(cos⁡2t)=−2sin⁡2tdydt=ddt(cos⁡t)=−sin⁡t.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t(−2sin⁡2t)2+(−sin⁡t)2dt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t4sin2⁡2t+sin2⁡tdt.

Now, using the identity sin⁡2t=2sin⁡tcos⁡t, we can rewrite our integral as follows:

S=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t4sin2⁡2t+sin2⁡tdt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t4(2sin⁡tcos⁡t)2+sin2⁡tdt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t16sin2⁡tcos2⁡t+sin2⁡tdt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡tsin2⁡t(16cos2⁡t+1)dt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t⋅sin2⁡t⋅16cos2⁡t+1dt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t⋅|sin⁡t|⋅16cos2⁡t+1dt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡tsin⁡t16cos2⁡t+1dt

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option d. Using S=2π∫y√((x′)²+(y′)²) dt, with x′=-2sin(2t) and y′=-sin(t), the speed simplifies to sin(t)√(16cos²(t)+1) because sin(t)≥0 on [0,π/4]. Multiplication by y=cos(t) gives the displayed integral in d. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option a.

content.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of X
content.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{4}].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡2t=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t(16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot |\operatorname{sin}⁡t|\cdot \sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t(16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot |\operatorname{sin}⁡t|\cdot \sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

S=∫2πyds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=π4.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(cos⁡2t)=−2sin⁡2tdydt=ddt(cos⁡t)=−sin⁡t.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t(−2sin⁡2t)2+(−sin⁡t)2dt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t4sin2⁡2t+sin2⁡tdt.

decision.explanation: Rotation about the x-axis gives S=2π∫y√((x′)²+(y′)²) dt. Here x′=-sin(t), y′=e^t, and y=e^t>0. Thus S=2π∫₀¹e^t√(sin²(t)+e^(2t)) dt, which is option a.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y={e}^{t},\,t\in [0,1].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=cos⁡t,y=et,t∈[0,1]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
2π∫01etsin2⁡t+e2tdt
b
2π∫01e2tsin⁡tdt
c
2π∫01et(sin⁡t+et)dt
d
2π∫01sin⁡tcos2⁡t+e2tdt
e
4π∫01tsin⁡t+etdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=1.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(cos⁡t)=−sin⁡tdydt=ddt(et)=et.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫01et(−sin⁡t)2+(et)2dt=2π∫01etsin2⁡t+e2tdt.

content.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of X
content.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y={e}^{t},\,t\in [0,1].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
history.html:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=1.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(cos⁡t)=−sin⁡tdydt=ddt(et)=et.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫01et(−sin⁡t)2+(et)2dt=2π∫01etsin2⁡t+e2tdt.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=5t+1,\,y={t}^{2},\,t\in [0,3].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=3.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t+1)=5 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{t}^{2}\sqrt{{(5)}^{2}+{(2t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{t}^{2}\sqrt{25+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=5t+1,y=t2,t∈[0,3]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
5π∫03t2(5t+1)dt
b
2π∫03t225+4t2dt
c
10π∫03t5+2t2dt
d
2π∫03(5t+1)25+2tdt
e
10π∫03t3dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=3.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(5t+1)=5dydt=ddt(t2)=2t.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫03t2(5)2+(2t)2dt=2π∫03t225+4t2dt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms b: x′=5 and y′=2t, so ds=√(25+4t²) dt. The radius about the x-axis is y=t², giving S=2π∫₀³t²√(25+4t²) dt. The incorrect feedback applies to the deliberately submitted option c.

content.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of X
content.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=5t+1,\,y={t}^{2},\,t\in [0,3].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=3.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t+1)=5 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{t}^{2}\sqrt{{(5)}^{2}+{(2t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{t}^{2}\sqrt{25+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 4
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=et,y=4t,t∈[0,2]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
16π∫02te2tdt
b
4π∫02etet+4dt
c
8π∫02te2t+16dt
d
8π∫02tet+16t2dt
e
8π∫02tetdt
Submit

decision.explanation: For rotation about the x-axis, S=2π∫y√((x′)²+(y′)²) dt. Here x′=e^t, y′=4, and y=4t≥0. Therefore S=8π∫₀²t√(e^(2t)+16) dt, matching option c.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={e}^{t},\,y=4t,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}4t\sqrt{{({e}^{t})}^{2}+{(4)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}t\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+16}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 4
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=et,y=4t,t∈[0,2]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
16π∫02te2tdt
b
4π∫02etet+4dt
c
8π∫02te2t+16dt
d
8π∫02tet+16t2dt
e
8π∫02tetdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=2.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(et)=etdydt=ddt(4t)=4.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫024t(et)2+(4)2dt=8π∫02te2t+16dt.

content.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of X
content.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={e}^{t},\,y=4t,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}4t\sqrt{{({e}^{t})}^{2}+{(4)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}t\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+16}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=t2+1,y=t3,t∈[0,2]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
2π∫02(t2+1)4t2+9tdt
b
4π∫02t4t3+t2+1dt
c
2π∫02t33t4+2dt
d
2π∫02t49t2+4dt
e
4π∫02t33t3+2tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: For rotation about the x-axis, S=2π∫y√((x′)²+(y′)²) dt. Here x′=2t and y′=3t², so the speed is √(4t²+9t⁴)=t√(4+9t²), since t≥0. Multiplying by y=t³ gives 2π∫₀²t⁴√(9t²+4) dt, which is option d.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{2}+1,\,y={t}^{3},\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)=2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})=3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{{t}^{2}(4+9{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{(4+9{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\cdot |t|\cdot \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\cdot t\cdot \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{4}\sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=t2+1,y=t3,t∈[0,2]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
2π∫02(t2+1)4t2+9tdt
b
4π∫02t4t3+t2+1dt
c
2π∫02t33t4+2dt
d
2π∫02t49t2+4dt
e
4π∫02t33t3+2tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=2.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(t2+1)=2tdydt=ddt(t3)=3t2.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫02t3(2t)2+(3t2)2dt=2π∫02t34t2+9t4dt=2π∫02t3t2(4+9t2)dt=2π∫02t3⋅t2⋅(4+9t2)dt=2π∫02t3⋅|t|⋅9t2+4dt=2π∫02t3⋅t⋅9t2+4dt=2π∫02t49t2+4dt.

content.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of X
content.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{2}+1,\,y={t}^{3},\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)=2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})=3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{{t}^{2}(4+9{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{(4+9{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\cdot |t|\cdot \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\cdot t\cdot \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{4}\sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=cosh⁡t,y=cosh⁡2t,t∈[0,2]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
8π∫02sinh⁡tcosh2⁡tdt
b
4π∫02sinh2⁡t1+8cosh2⁡tdt
c
2π∫02sinh⁡tcosh⁡t1+16cosh2⁡tdt
d
4π∫02sinh⁡2tdt
e
8π∫02sinh⁡tcosh⁡2t1+4cosh2⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: About the y-axis, S=2π∫x√((x′)²+(y′)²) dt. Here x′=sinh(t) and y′=2sinh(2t)=4sinh(t)cosh(t). Since sinh(t)≥0 on [0,2], the speed is sinh(t)√(1+16cosh²(t)). Multiplying by x=cosh(t) gives option c.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cosh}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{cosh}⁡2t,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cosh}⁡t)=\operatorname{sinh}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cosh}⁡2t)=2\operatorname{sinh}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sinh}⁡t)}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡2t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t+4{sinh}^{2}⁡2t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\operatorname{sinh}⁡2t=2\operatorname{sinh}⁡t\operatorname{cosh}⁡t,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t+4{sinh}^{2}⁡2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t+4(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡t\operatorname{cosh}⁡t)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t+16{sinh}^{2}⁡t{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t(1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \sqrt{1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\cdot |\operatorname{sinh}⁡t|\cdot \sqrt{1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{sinh}⁡t\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=cosh⁡t,y=cosh⁡2t,t∈[0,2]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
8π∫02sinh⁡tcosh2⁡tdt
b
4π∫02sinh2⁡t1+8cosh2⁡tdt
c
2π∫02sinh⁡tcosh⁡t1+16cosh2⁡tdt
d
4π∫02sinh⁡2tdt
e
8π∫02sinh⁡tcosh⁡2t1+4cosh2⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis using the formula

S=∫2πxds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=2.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(cosh⁡t)=sinh⁡tdydt=ddt(cosh⁡2t)=2sinh⁡2t.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫02cosh⁡t(sinh⁡t)2+(2sinh⁡2t)2dt=2π∫02cosh⁡tsinh2⁡t+4sinh2⁡2tdt.

Now, using the identity sinh⁡2t=2sinh⁡tcosh⁡t, we can rewrite our integral as follows:

S=2π∫02cosh⁡tsinh2⁡t+4sinh2⁡2tdt=2π∫02cosh⁡tsinh2⁡t+4(2sinh⁡tcosh⁡t)2dt=2π∫02cosh⁡tsinh2⁡t+16sinh2⁡tcosh2⁡tdt=2π∫02cosh⁡tsinh2⁡t(1+16cosh2⁡t)dt=2π∫02cosh⁡t⋅sinh2⁡t⋅1+16cosh2⁡tdt=2π∫02cosh⁡t⋅|sinh⁡t|⋅1+16cosh2⁡tdt=2π∫02sinh⁡tcosh⁡t1+16cosh2⁡tdt

content.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y
content.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cosh}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{cosh}⁡2t,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cosh}⁡t)=\operatorname{sinh}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cosh}⁡2t)=2\operatorname{sinh}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sinh}⁡t)}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡2t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t+4{sinh}^{2}⁡2t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\operatorname{sinh}⁡2t=2\operatorname{sinh}⁡t\operatorname{cosh}⁡t,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t+4{sinh}^{2}⁡2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t+4(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡t\operatorname{cosh}⁡t)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t+16{sinh}^{2}⁡t{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t(1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{{sinh}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \sqrt{1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\cdot |\operatorname{sinh}⁡t|\cdot \sqrt{1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{sinh}⁡t\operatorname{cosh}⁡t\sqrt{1+16{cosh}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=2sin⁡t,y=2cos⁡t,t∈[0,π]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
22π∫0πsin2⁡tdt
b
8π∫0πsin⁡tdt
c
4π∫0πcos2⁡tdt
d
8π∫0πcos⁡tdt
e
22π∫0πsin⁡tcos⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: About the y-axis, S=2π∫|x|√((x′)²+(y′)²) dt. Here x′=2cos(t), y′=-2sin(t), so the speed is 2. Since x=2sin(t)≥0 on [0,π], S=8π∫₀^πsin(t) dt, matching option b.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\pi ].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\pi .$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 2\cdot \sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity ${sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t=1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=2sin⁡t,y=2cos⁡t,t∈[0,π]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
22π∫0πsin2⁡tdt
b
8π∫0πsin⁡tdt
c
4π∫0πcos2⁡tdt
d
8π∫0πcos⁡tdt
e
22π∫0πsin⁡tcos⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis using the formula

S=∫2πxds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=π.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(2sin⁡t)=2cos⁡tdydt=ddt(2cos⁡t)=−2sin⁡t.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫0π2sin⁡t(2cos⁡t)2+(−2sin⁡t)2dt=4π∫0πsin⁡t4cos2⁡t+4sin2⁡tdt=4π∫0πsin⁡t4(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)dt=4π∫0πsin⁡t⋅2⋅sin2⁡t+cos2⁡tdt=8π∫0πsin⁡tsin2⁡t+cos2⁡tdt.

Now, using the identity sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t=1, we can rewrite our integral as follows:

S=8π∫0πsin⁡tsin2⁡t+cos2⁡tdt=8π∫0πsin⁡tdt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option b. The radius is x=2sin(t)≥0, and the speed is √(4cos²(t)+4sin²(t))=2. Thus S=2π∫₀^π(2sin(t))(2) dt=8π∫₀^πsin(t) dt. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option e.

content.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y
content.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\pi ].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\pi .$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 2\cdot \sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity ${sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t=1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 8
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=t3,y=2t,t∈[0,2]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
4π∫02t3t4+2dt
b
6π∫02t5dt
c
2π∫02tt4+2dt
d
4π∫02t3t2+1dt
e
2π∫02t39t4+4dt
Submit

decision.explanation: About the y-axis, S=2π∫|x|√((x′)²+(y′)²) dt. Here x=t³≥0, x′=3t², and y′=2. Thus S=2π∫₀²t³√(9t⁴+4) dt, matching option e.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{3},\,y=2t,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})=3{t}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}+{(2)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=t3,y=2t,t∈[0,2]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
4π∫02t3t4+2dt
b
6π∫02t5dt
c
2π∫02tt4+2dt
d
4π∫02t3t2+1dt
e
2π∫02t39t4+4dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis using the formula

S=∫2πxds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=2.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(t3)=3t2dydt=ddt(2t)=2.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫02t3(3t2)2+(2)2dt=2π∫02t39t4+4dt.

content.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y
content.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{3},\,y=2t,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})=3{t}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}+{(2)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=cos2⁡t,y=sin2⁡t,t∈[0,π2]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
4π∫0π/2sin2⁡tcos2⁡tdt
b
22π∫0π/2sin⁡tcos⁡tdt
c
8π∫0π/2cos3⁡tdt
d
2π∫0π/2sin2⁡tcos⁡tdt
e
42π∫0π/2sin⁡tcos3⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: About the y-axis, S=2π∫x√((x′)²+(y′)²) dt. Here x′=-2sin(t)cos(t) and y′=2sin(t)cos(t), giving speed 2√2 sin(t)cos(t) on [0,π/2]. Multiplying by x=cos²(t) yields option e.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={cos}^{2}⁡t,\,y={sin}^{2}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({cos}^{2}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{2}⁡t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{8{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\cdot |\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t|\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=cos2⁡t,y=sin2⁡t,t∈[0,π2]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
4π∫0π/2sin2⁡tcos2⁡tdt
b
22π∫0π/2sin⁡tcos⁡tdt
c
8π∫0π/2cos3⁡tdt
d
2π∫0π/2sin2⁡tcos⁡tdt
e
42π∫0π/2sin⁡tcos3⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis using the formula

S=∫2πxds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=π2.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(cos2⁡t)=−2sin⁡tcos⁡tdydt=ddt(sin2⁡t)=2sin⁡tcos⁡t.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫0π/2cos2⁡t(−2sin⁡tcos⁡t)2+(2sin⁡tcos⁡t)2dt=2π∫0π/2cos2⁡t4sin2⁡tcos2⁡t+4sin2⁡tcos2⁡tdt=2π∫0π/2cos2⁡t8sin2⁡tcos2⁡tdt=2π∫0π/2cos2⁡t⋅22⋅|sin⁡tcos⁡t|dt=42π∫0π/2cos2⁡t⋅sin⁡tcos⁡tdt=42π∫0π/2sin⁡tcos3⁡tdt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms e: the radius is cos²(t), and the speed is 2√2 sin(t)cos(t), giving 4√2π∫₀^(π/2)sin(t)cos³(t) dt. Option b happens to have the same integral value, √2π, but e directly expresses the surface-area formula.

content.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y
content.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={cos}^{2}⁡t,\,y={sin}^{2}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({cos}^{2}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{2}⁡t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{8{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\cdot |\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t|\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=3t,y=et,t∈[0,3]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
2π∫033t9tln2⁡3+e2tdt
b
6πln⁡3∫033te2tdt
c
6π∫0332t3tln⁡3+etdt
d
2π∫03et3tln⁡3+etdt
e
2πln⁡3∫0332tetdt
Submit

decision.explanation: About the y-axis, S=2π∫x√((x′)²+(y′)²) dt. Here x′=3^t ln(3) and y′=e^t, so (x′)²=9^t(ln(3))². Multiplying the speed by the radius x=3^t gives option a.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={3}^{t},\,y={e}^{t},\,t\in [0,3].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=3.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({3}^{t})={3}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{3}^{t}\sqrt{{({3}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡3)}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{3}^{t}\sqrt{{3}^{2t}{ln}^{2}⁡3+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{3}^{t}\sqrt{{9}^{t}{ln}^{2}⁡3+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=3t,y=et,t∈[0,3]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis?

a
2π∫033t9tln2⁡3+e2tdt
b
6πln⁡3∫033te2tdt
c
6π∫0332t3tln⁡3+etdt
d
2π∫03et3tln⁡3+etdt
e
2πln⁡3∫0332tetdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis using the formula

S=∫2πxds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=3.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(3t)=3tln⁡3dydt=ddt(et)=et.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫033t(3tln⁡3)2+(et)2dt=2π∫033t32tln2⁡3+e2tdt=2π∫033t9tln2⁡3+e2tdt.

content.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y
content.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={3}^{t},\,y={e}^{t},\,t\in [0,3].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=3.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({3}^{t})={3}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{3}^{t}\sqrt{{({3}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡3)}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{3}^{t}\sqrt{{3}^{2t}{ln}^{2}⁡3+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{3}^{t}\sqrt{{9}^{t}{ln}^{2}⁡3+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={e}^{t}-t,\,y=4{e}^{t/2},\,t\in [0,\operatorname{ln}⁡4].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡4.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}-t)={e}^{t}-1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{e}^{t/2})=2{e}^{t/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{({e}^{t}-1)}^{2}+{(2{e}^{t/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{t}+1+4{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{({e}^{t}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}({e}^{t}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}8\pi {e}^{t/2}({e}^{t}+1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u={e}^{t/2}.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{t/2}\,\text{d}t,$ or $2\,\text{d}u={e}^{t/2}\,\text{d}t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}8\pi ({e}^{t}+1)\cdot {e}^{t/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}8\pi ({u}^{2}+1)\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({u}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\pi {[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+u]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =16\pi ((\frac{8}{3}+2)-(\frac{1}{3}+1)) \\  & =16\pi (\frac{14}{3}-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =16\pi (\frac{10}{3}) \\  & =\frac{160\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, S=2π∫0ln⁡44et/2(et−1)2+(2et/2)2dt=2π∫0ln⁡44et/2e2t−2et+1+4etdt=2π∫0ln⁡44et/2e2t+2et+1dt=2π∫0ln⁡44et/2(et+1)2dt=2π∫0ln⁡44et/2(et+1)dt=∫0ln⁡48πet/2(et+1)dt.

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution u=et/2. Then, du=12et/2dt, or 2du=et/2dt. We also update the limits of integration for u:

t 0 ln⁡4
u 1 2

Therefore, we get S=∫0ln⁡48π(et+1)⋅et/2dt=∫128π(u2+1)⋅2du=16π∫12(u2+1)du=16π[u33+u]12=16π((83+2)−(13+1))=16π(143−43)=16π(103)=160π3.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms S=160π/3. The speed simplifies to e^t+1, so S=8π∫₀^(ln 4)e^(t/2)(e^t+1) dt. Substituting u=e^(t/2) gives 16π∫₁²(u²+1) du=160π/3. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted 80π/3.

content.knowledge_point: Computing a Surface Area of Revolution
content.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={e}^{t}-t,\,y=4{e}^{t/2},\,t\in [0,\operatorname{ln}⁡4].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}
content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡4.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}-t)={e}^{t}-1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{e}^{t/2})=2{e}^{t/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{({e}^{t}-1)}^{2}+{(2{e}^{t/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{t}+1+4{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{({e}^{t}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}({e}^{t}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}8\pi {e}^{t/2}({e}^{t}+1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u={e}^{t/2}.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{t/2}\,\text{d}t,$ or $2\,\text{d}u={e}^{t/2}\,\text{d}t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}8\pi ({e}^{t}+1)\cdot {e}^{t/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}8\pi ({u}^{2}+1)\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({u}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\pi {[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+u]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =16\pi ((\frac{8}{3}+2)-(\frac{1}{3}+1)) \\  & =16\pi (\frac{14}{3}-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =16\pi (\frac{10}{3}) \\  & =\frac{160\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The radius is x=e^t−t>0, and the speed is √((e^t−1)²+4e^t)=e^t+1. Thus S=2π∫₀¹(e^t−t)(e^t+1) dt=2π[(1/2)e^(2t)+(2−t)e^t−t²/2]₀¹=(e²+2e−6)π, matching option e.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={e}^{t}-t,\,y=4{e}^{t/2},\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}-t)={e}^{t}-1 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{e}^{t/2})=2{e}^{t/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{({e}^{t}-1)}^{2}+{(2{e}^{t/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{t}+1+4{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression ${e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{({e}^{t}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\cdot |{e}^{t}+1|\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\cdot ({e}^{t}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-t{e}^{t}-t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi [{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t]\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t$ using integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{t} & ⇒ & v={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}x & =t{e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =t{e}^{t}-{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi [{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t] \\  & =2\pi [{(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})|}_{0}^{1}-{(t{e}^{t}-{e}^{t})|}_{0}^{1}] \\  & =2\pi [(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+e-\frac{1}{2})-(\frac{1}{2}+1-0)-(e-e)+(0-1)] \\  & =2\pi [\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+e-3] \\  & =({e}^{2}+2e-6)\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=et−t,y=4et/2,t∈[0,1]. Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis.

a
 (2e2−e+3)π
b
 (e2+6e)π
c
 (e2+3e−1)π
d
 (e2−3)π
e
 (e2+2e−6)π
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis using the formula

S=∫2πxds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=1.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(et−t)=et−1dydt=ddt(4et/2)=2et/2.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2x(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫01(et−t)(et−1)2+(2et/2)2dt=2π∫01(et−t)e2t−2et+1+4etdt=2π∫01(et−t)e2t+2et+1dt

Now, factoring the expression e2t+2et+1, we can rewrite our integral as follows:

S=2π∫01(et−t)e2t+2et+1dt=2π∫01(et−t)(et+1)2dt=2π∫01(et−t)⋅|et+1|dt=2π∫01(et−t)⋅(et+1)dt=2π∫01(e2t+et−tet−t)dt=2π[∫01(e2t+et−t)dt−∫01tetdt]

We evaluate the integral ∫01tetdt using integration by parts. We set u=t⇒u′=1v′=et⇒v=et.

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get ∫tetdx=tet−∫et⋅1dx=tet−et.

Therefore, we get

S=2π[∫01(e2t+et−t)dt−∫01tetdt]=2π[(12e2t+et−12t2)|01−(tet−et)|01]=2π[(12e2+e−12)−(12+1−0)−(e−e)+(0−1)]=2π[12e2+e−3]=(e2+2e−6)π.

content.knowledge_point: Computing a Surface Area of Revolution
content.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={e}^{t}-t,\,y=4{e}^{t/2},\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}-t)={e}^{t}-1 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{e}^{t/2})=2{e}^{t/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{({e}^{t}-1)}^{2}+{(2{e}^{t/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{t}+1+4{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression ${e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\sqrt{({e}^{t}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\cdot |{e}^{t}+1|\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{t}-t)\cdot ({e}^{t}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-t{e}^{t}-t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi [{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t]\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t$ using integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{t} & ⇒ & v={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}x & =t{e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =t{e}^{t}-{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi [{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t] \\  & =2\pi [{(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}+{e}^{t}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})|}_{0}^{1}-{(t{e}^{t}-{e}^{t})|}_{0}^{1}] \\  & =2\pi [(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+e-\frac{1}{2})-(\frac{1}{2}+1-0)-(e-e)+(0-1)] \\  & =2\pi [\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+e-3] \\  & =({e}^{2}+2e-6)\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=3t2,y=2t3,t∈[0,3]. Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the y-axis.

a
 910π3
b
696π5
c
 142π5
d
 112π5
e
 1126π3
Submit

decision.explanation: The speed is √((6t)²+(6t²)²)=6t√(1+t²), and the radius about the y-axis is 3t². Thus S=36π∫₀^√3 t³√(1+t²) dt. With u=1+t², this becomes 18π∫₁⁴(u−1)√u du=18π[(2/5)u^(5/2)−(2/3)u^(3/2)]₁⁴=696π/5, matching b.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=3{t}^{2},\,y=2{t}^{3},\,t\in [0,\sqrt{3}].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt{3}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})=6t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3})=6{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{{(6t)}^{2}+{(6{t}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{36{t}^{2}+36{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression $36{t}^{2}+36{t}^{4},$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{36{t}^{2}+36{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t] \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{36{t}^{2}(1+{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\cdot |6t|\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\cdot 6t\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}2{t}^{3}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+{t}^{2}$ Then, ${t}^{2}=u-1$ and $\text{d}u=2t\,\text{d}t.$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\sqrt{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$

content.knowledge_point: Computing a Surface Area of Revolution
content.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=3{t}^{2},\,y=2{t}^{3},\,t\in [0,\sqrt{3}].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt{3}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})=6t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3})=6{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{{(6t)}^{2}+{(6{t}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{36{t}^{2}+36{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression $36{t}^{2}+36{t}^{4},$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{36{t}^{2}+36{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t] \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{36{t}^{2}(1+{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\cdot |6t|\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3{t}^{2}\cdot 6t\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}2{t}^{3}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+{t}^{2}$ Then, ${t}^{2}=u-1$ and $\text{d}u=2t\,\text{d}t.$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\sqrt{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}2{t}^{3}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}2t\cdot {t}^{2}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}(u-1)\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}(u-1){u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}({u}^{3/2}-{u}^{1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =18\pi \cdot {[\frac{2{u}^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =18\pi [(\frac{2({4}^{5/2})}{5}-\frac{2({4}^{3/2})}{3})-(\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{3})] \\  & =18\pi \cdot [(\frac{64}{5}-\frac{16}{3})-(\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{3})) \\  & =18\pi \cdot (\frac{62}{5}-\frac{14}{3}) \\  & =18\pi \cdot \frac{116}{15} \\  & =\frac{696\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-2{t}^{3})=6-6{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2})=12t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Now, factoring the expression $36{t}^{4}+72{t}^{2}+36,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}6{t}^{2}\sqrt{36({t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}6{t}^{2}\cdot 6\sqrt{{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =72\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\sqrt{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =72\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\cdot |{t}^{2}+1|\,\text{d}t \\  & =72\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =72\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{4}+{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =72\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{4}+{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =72\pi \cdot {[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =72\pi [(\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{3})-(\frac{0}{5}+\frac{0}{3})] \\  & =72\pi \cdot \frac{8}{15} \\  & =\frac{192\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
